Ben Jonson, in the First Folio, 1623 You have walked his life from the glover's house in Henley Street to the stone in Holy Trinity, and watched his fellows gather the plays so that they would not be lost. Walk his life again from the start
The Folio Library, 1623
William Shakespeare, 1564 to 1616 · from the records, his own words, and Sidney Lee's Life of 1899 🪶 The Player's Life
You have walked his whole life. Your keepsakes:

In the Folio Library at Stationers' Hall, two old players are gathering his plays into one great book, seven years after his death. Walk the life behind it, as the records tell it: Stratford, the road to London, the Rose and the Theatre, the Globe built and burned, Whitehall and Blackfriars, and home again.
chapters, all over London and Stratford, about four hours and more at your own pace. Where nobody knows what happened, the book says so. Your place is kept.
▶ Begin: the Folio Library, 1623
Back to where you were
Stationers' Hall, by St Paul's
Walk it again from the start
A proof page of the Folio
Stationers' Hall, by St Paul's, in the autumn of 1623
Seven years after William Shakespeare died, two of the players who had worked beside him for twenty years are gathering his plays into one great book, so that they will not be lost.

John Heminges, about 57, in 1623: player with Shakespeare's company since the 1590s, its business manager, a grocer by trade, father of many children. With Henry Condell he is gathering Shakespeare's plays into the First Folio 'only to keep the memory of so worthy a friend and fellow alive, as was our Shakespeare'. Kind, careful, proud of the work, a little tired.
Ah, mind the sheets, they are still damp from the press. We are making a book of our friend's plays. Thirty-six of them.

Henry Condell, player of the King's Men in 1623, Heminges's partner in gathering the First Folio. Shakespeare left him 26 shillings and 8 pence in his will to buy a memorial ring. Warm, plain-spoken, fond of Will.
You've come to see the great book? Eighteen of these plays were never printed before. Without this, Macbeth and The Tempest would be gone.
John Heminges is gathering the plays. Ask him why.

'We have done this office to the dead only to keep the memory of so worthy a friend and fellow alive, as was our Shakespeare. His mind and hand went together: and what he thought, he uttered with that easiness, that we have scarce received from him a blot in his papers.' (from their letter at the front of the Folio, 1623)
Henry Condell has a word for the readers. Hear it.
📜 To the great Variety of Readers

'Read him, therefore; and again, and again: and if then you do not like him, surely you are in some manifest danger, not to understand him.' Condell taps the pile of sheets. 'Comedies, histories and tragedies. Some of these were only ever in the prompt books, cut and scribbled on. We have put them right as best we could.'
▶ Look at the sheets
The First Folio (1623)
Look at the First Folio on its lectern: every word, as they printed it.
Heminges counts on his fingers. 'All the plays we could gather, in one volume. How many?'
Sixteen are the plays you can walk in this world. The Folio has more than twice that.
There are 154 sonnets, but the Folio has no sonnets in it at all.
'And we have sorted them into three kinds, as the title says.' Which three?
Comedies, Histories and Tragedies
Plays, Poems and Sonnets
Romances, Masques and Jigs
No poems are in the Folio. It is all plays.
Masques and jigs were played, but nobody printed them as his.
Heminges's dropped quill
Heminges has dropped his quill on the floor by the press sheets. Pick it up for him.
Give Heminges back his quill.
🪶 Where it begins

'Thank you. Now, if you want to know who he was, you must go back to the beginning: a glover's house in Henley Street, Stratford-upon-Avon, in the spring of 1564. Go and see. Then come back to us; we shall still be at it.'
Out into Paul's Churchyard, by the door of Stationers' Hall.
A bookseller of Paul's Churchyard
Ask the bookseller in Paul's Churchyard what such a great book will cost.

'The great Shakespeare book? Isaac Jaggard and Edward Blount have it in hand. About a pound, I'd say, bound in calf: weeks of wages for a craftsman. And worth it. But the man himself, now: they say his father was a glover in Stratford, and he came up to London with nothing.'
Take the carrier's wagon from the Tabard Inn in Southwark to Stratford-upon-Avon. Walk over London Bridge to it.
A glover's thimble
Henley Street, Stratford-upon-Avon
William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in April 1564, the son of John Shakespeare, a glover and wool dealer, and Mary Arden, a farmer's daughter.
Mary Shakespeare (Mary Arden)
John Shakespeare, glover

Mary Shakespeare, born Mary Arden, about 30 in 1570: youngest daughter of Robert Arden, a well-off farmer of Wilmcote, who left her land. Mother of eight children; two daughters died as babies before William was born, and he survived the plague that came to Stratford in the summer of 1564. Practical, warm, careful with money, proud of her husband's place in the town.
Wipe your feet, there's leather all over this floor. Are you looking for my husband or my boy?
Go into the house on Henley Street. Mary Shakespeare is at home.

'He was baptised on the 26th of April, at Holy Trinity. That summer the plague came to Stratford. One in eight of the town died before Christmas, and we kept him in and prayed. He lived. Two of my girls before him did not.' She says it plainly, and goes back to her work.
Talk to John Shakespeare, glover, at his bench.

'Glover and whittawer: I dress the soft white leather myself. And bailiff of this town in 1568, that is to say mayor, if you please. When the Queen's players came that year, it was I who paid them out of the town's purse to play in the Guildhall. My boy stood at my knee and watched. Never took his eyes off them.'
Make a pair of gloves with John: press E at John and choose 'learn to make gloves'.
The birthroom stair
Read about the house at the birthroom stair.
Out into Henley Street.
Go up into the King's New School over the Guildhall, and take the hornbook lesson from the schoolmaster.
🏫 The grammar school
Boys here learned Latin from about seven, from six in the morning in summer. In the parish register, in Latin, he is Gulielmus filius Johannes Shakspere . What is Gulielmus?
'Johannes' is John, his father.
Down the stair and out of the school.
The parish clerk of Holy Trinity
Walk down to Holy Trinity by the river and ask the parish clerk to show you the register.

'Here, April 1564: Gulielmus filius Johannes Shakspere , baptised the 26th. Nobody wrote down his birthday; folk say the 23rd, Saint George's Day. And here, in July: Hic incepit pestis , here the plague began. Look how the burials run on down the page after it.'
Someone has left a child's glove on a pew, of the soft white leather John Shakespeare makes. Pick it up; it will go back to Henley Street.
Shottery and Stratford, 1582 to 1585
A sprig of wedding rosemary
Anne Shakespeare (Anne Hathaway)
Shottery, a mile west of the town, November 1582
In November 1582, at eighteen, William married Anne Hathaway of Shottery, who was twenty-six. Their daughter Susanna was baptised six months later, and in 1585 the twins, Hamnet and Judith.

Fulk Sandells, farmer of Shottery, in November 1582: a friend of Anne Hathaway's late father Richard. With John Richardson he rode to Worcester on 28 November 1582 to stand surety for forty pounds so that William Shakespeare could marry Anne after only one calling of the banns. Plain, steady, a little stiff about it all.
Good day. Mind the geese.

Hamnet Sadler, baker of Stratford, about 1585: William Shakespeare's good friend and neighbour; with his wife Judith he stood godparent to William's twins, who were named Hamnet and Judith after them. Shakespeare remembered him in his will thirty years later. Cheerful, floury, kind.
Morning! Bread's still warm.
Talk to Anne Hathaway outside her family's farmhouse at Shottery.

'Hewlands, my father called the farm. He died last year and left me six pounds thirteen shillings and fourpence, to be paid on my wedding day. Will is eighteen. I am twenty-six. Folk will count the months, and let them count: the child is coming in the spring, and we shall be married first.'
Fulk Sandells rode to Worcester for the licence. Ask him about it.

'Twenty-eighth of November. John Richardson and I put our names to a bond of forty pound at the Bishop's court in Worcester: that there's no reason in law the young man shouldn't marry Anne, after the banns are asked but once. Forty pound! More than the farm makes in a year. Well. Richard Hathaway would have wanted it done properly.'
Anne was born in 1556, Will in 1564. When they married in 1582, how much older was she?
Eighteen was Will's own age.
Rosemary from the garden
Gather rosemary from Anne's garden: it was carried at weddings, for remembering.
A sprig of rosemary.
Bring Anne the rosemary.
'Thank you. Rosemary for remembrance.' She tucks it in her bodice. Their daughter Susanna was baptised on the 26th of May, 1583. And on the 2nd of February 1585, twins: a boy and a girl.
Walk into the town and find Hamnet Sadler the baker, Will's friend.

'Twins! And named for my wife and me: Hamnet and Judith. We stood for them at the font. Will's over the moon, and terrified. Three little ones and no trade of his own. His father's business is going downhill, you know; John's in debt, and he has stopped coming to the council.'
Who were the twins named after?
Their godparents, Hamnet and Judith Sadler
Two characters in a play
Will's own brother and sister
He had written no plays yet; that was years away.
His brothers were Gilbert, Richard and Edmund; his sister was Joan.
Go to Holy Trinity and see the twins' names in the register.

' Hamnet & Judeth, sonne and daughter to William Shakspere. There they are.' The clerk turns a page. 'And after that, hardly a word of Will Shakespeare in any record anywhere, for seven years. Where he went, nobody knows.'
From Stratford to London: the road nobody wrote down
Between the baptism of his twins in 1585 and 1592, when he was already known in London as a writer of plays, there is no record of William Shakespeare at all. These are the lost years.
A player of the Queen's Men

One of the Queen's Men, the most famous company of players in England, on tour in the summer of 1587. They played in Stratford that year. In June at Thame in Oxfordshire one of the company, William Knell, was killed in a fight with a fellow player, John Towne, so the company was a man short. A travelling player: quick, worldly, tired of the road. He does not know Will Shakespeare's future, and nobody does.
The Queen's Men, at your service, friend. We play the Guildhall tonight.

Richard Field, printer of Blackfriars, London, about 1590: born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1561, the son of a tanner who knew John Shakespeare; apprenticed to a London printer and married his master's widow. In 1593 he will print Venus and Adonis for his townsman. Careful, learned, proud of his fine type.
A Stratford voice! Come in, come in, but don't touch the formes.
The Queen's Men have come to Stratford. Talk to their player by the carrier's wagon.

'We are a man short, friend. William Knell, one of our best, was killed at Thame in June: a quarrel with John Towne, swords out, and Towne stabbed him in the neck. Knell's dead, Towne's pardoned. That's the truth of it.' He looks you up and down. 'You've a good voice. Some young man in this town has, too, I hear.'
Between 1585 and 1592, what do the records say Will Shakespeare did?
Nothing: nobody knows
He was a schoolmaster in the country
He fled Stratford for poaching deer
John Aubrey heard that, eighty years later, from an old actor's son. It may be true; no record shows it.
That tale was first told a hundred years later. No record shows it.
Take the carrier's wagon to London, the way so many young men from Stratford went.
Walk north up Borough High Street onto London Bridge, with its houses built all along it.
Stand on the bridge. On the gate at the Southwark end, the heads of traitors were set on poles. Look at the river: the busiest road in London.
Cross into the City and find the Print Shop at the Sign of the Green Dragon by St Paul's. Set a line of type and print a page.
Richard Field from Stratford is visiting the printer. Talk to him.

'Our fathers knew each other: mine was a tanner in Bridge Street. I came up in 1579, to be a printer's apprentice. Now I have my own shop in Blackfriars. Plenty of Stratford lads come up to London. If your friend writes anything worth printing, send him to me.'
A penny on the floor
There's a penny on the print shop floor: the price of standing in a playhouse yard. Pick it up.
Out into the street.
Walk back over the bridge to Bankside, to the Rose playhouse, the newest in London.
The Rose, Bankside, March 1592
On the 3rd of March 1592 a new play, Henry VI, was acted at the Rose. It was a triumph. By the autumn, a jealous older writer was calling its young author an 'upstart Crow'.
If you've come about the Greene pamphlet: I'm sorry for it, and I've said so in print.
Read Philip Henslowe's diary, his account book, in the Rose.
Ask Philip Henslowe how the new play did.
Twelve pence made a shilling, and twenty shillings a pound. How many pence is £3 16s 8d?
Out onto Bankside.
A Groatsworth of Wit
🐦 An upstart Crow
